Molecular dynamics follows atoms through time. We have seen how its predictions depend on the integration step, the surroundings, and the potential. Can we do anything fancier? The answer depends on the question. We may want the equilibrium arrangement of an alloy without following every vibration. We may want to follow composition changes across a microstructure too large to describe atom by atom. Or we may need more information about the electrons because the available potential misses an important interaction.

Unit 6 develops these possibilities through three connected questions.

1. **What arrangement does an alloy adopt when MD is too slow to show it?** Atoms in a solid alloy exchange sites far more rarely than MD can follow. We skip the path and evaluate the equilibrium average directly. It is an integral over every atomic coordinate, so we estimate it from random samples and ask how accurate that estimate is.
2. **Why do A and B not simply mix at random?** Sampling swaps on a lattice answers this, and comparing with the regular-solution model of Assignment 2 shows what that model misses. When the pattern grows larger than any lattice we can sample, we replace atoms by a concentration field that evolves in time.
3. **Can a fitted potential contain more atomic information?** The cluster-energy fitting in Assignment 2 provides a starting point. We follow a copper configuration from an electronic calculation to energy and force data, then ask how a flexible fitted model can supply forces for MD.

## [L27 · Monte Carlo techniques](L27/index.qmd) {#l27-sampling}

The unit follows one problem: a Cu–Ag alloy, quenched from a mixed state, separates into Cu-rich and Ag-rich regions [@xu2022cunanowires]. Our first attempt uses MD with an EAM potential for Cu–Ag [@williams2006embedded] on a GPU. The atoms vibrate but never hop, because measured copper self-diffusion at 1000 K gives one hop about every 5 µs, while a day of MD covers 46 ns [@kuper1954selfdiffusion]. Monte Carlo skips the vibrations and simulates the hops as random events. We connect this idea to Buffon's needle from Unit 1 and to its origin at Los Alamos [@metropolis1987beginning], learn to draw random events with seeds in NumPy, and write a lattice Monte Carlo in pure Python that measures a diffusion coefficient. With a constant hop probability the alloy stays mixed, and a micrometre-scale region would need about \(10^{14}\) attempts.

## [L28 · From Monte Carlo to continuum modeling](L28/index.qmd) {#l28-patterns}

We apply the same acceptance rule to A–B swaps on a lattice and ask how to make it fast enough for a microstructure. Following the Buffon acceleration of L04, we compare a serial loop, a vectorized update, and a GPU version that runs in the browser. Swaps share neighbours, so parallel updates must use non-touching pairs, which turns the sampler into a cellular automaton [@wolfram1983statistical].

The larger gain comes from changing the model. Averaging the lattice gives a composition field, and the Cahn–Hilliard equation describes its conserved evolution with the regular-solution free energy of [Assignment 2](../../assignments/A2/index.qmd), an interface cost, and a mobility [@cahn1958free; @cahn1961spinodal]. The L17 stencil turns it into coupled ODEs, and we compare forward Euler with a semi-implicit Fourier step [@chen1998applications].

## [L29 · Atomistic methods](L29/index.qmd) {#l29-atomic-data}

In [Assignment 2](../../assignments/A2/index.qmd), an energy residual determined the Lennard–Jones parameters. The larger held-out clusters tested how that fit transferred to a new environment. The optional copper-fitting project also provides energies and forces for distorted crystals and surfaces.

We examine where such reference data come from, using the electron density around fixed nuclei to introduce density functional theory [@kohn1965selfconsistent]. We then connect energy fitting, force fitting, and the choice of validation structures to a machine-learned interatomic potential [@behler2007generalized]. The final step returns to the MD loop: the fitted model supplies energy and its position derivatives, while the integrator still advances the atoms.

These three lectures complete the teaching sequence before the separate final review.
